summary.text: Take the composite squarefree number \(n=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341=23492890653051\), whose factors are all prime. Multiplicativity of the gcd-sum and its prime value \(2p-1\) give \(\sum_{k=1}^n\gcd(k,n)=610815156979325=26n-1\), so the relevant gcd is \(n\) and hence \(a(n)=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),\qquad
 a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+A(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit the composite positive integer
\[
n=23492890653051
\]
for which \(a(n)=1\). This disproves the proposed equivalence.

First we derive a convenient formula for the gcd-sum. For every positive integer \(n\),
\[
A(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d),                                      \tag{1}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function.

Indeed, reduction modulo \(n\) gives a bijection from the integers \(1,2,\ldots,n\) to the residues \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\): the integer \(n\) corresponds to residue \(0\), and every other integer corresponds to itself. Moreover,
\[
\gcd(k,n)=\gcd(k\bmod n,n).
\]
Thus \(A(n)\) is also the sum of \(\gcd(r,n)\) over \(0\le r<n\). Fix a divisor \(d\) of \(n\). The equality \(\gcd(r,n)=d\) is equivalent to writing \(r=du\), with \(0\le u<n/d\), and requiring
\[
\gcd(u,n/d)=1.
\]
There are exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) such residues \(u\). (This also covers \(d=n\): modulo \(1\) there is one residue, and \(\varphi(1)=1\).) Each corresponding gcd contributes \(d\), so summing over all divisors \(d\mid n\) proves (1).

Define
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d).
\]
The function \(G\) is multiplicative. To see this directly, suppose \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime. Every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(ef\), where \(e\mid m\) and \(f\mid n\). Furthermore, \(m/e\) and \(n/f\) are coprime. Since Euler's totient is multiplicative on coprime arguments,
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(mn)
 &=\sum_{e\mid m}\sum_{f\mid n}ef\,
   \varphi\!\left(\frac m e\frac n f\right)\\
 &=\sum_{e\mid m}\sum_{f\mid n}
   \left(e\varphi(m/e)\right)\left(f\varphi(n/f)\right)\\
 &=G(m)G(n).
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{2}
\]
If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), and therefore
\[
G(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1.                                  \tag{3}
\]

We now use the factorization
\[
\begin{aligned}
23492890653051
 &=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341.                                  \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, the successive products are
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\quad111\cdot43=4773,
\quad4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
and
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]
All five displayed factors in (4) are distinct primes. The small cases can be checked by trial division. Here is also a compact primality check that includes the two large factors.

We use the following standard Lucas criterion. Suppose the complete prime factorization of \(N-1\) is known. If an integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N
\]
and, for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(N-1\),
\[
\gcd\left(b^{(N-1)/q}-1,N\right)=1,
\]
then \(N\) is prime. To justify the criterion, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(N\). The order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divides \(N-1\), while the gcd conditions force this order to contain the full power of every prime occurring in \(N-1\). Hence the order is \(N-1\). Since an element of \((\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z)^\times\) has order at most \(r-1\), we get \(r\ge N\). As \(r\mid N\), this forces \(r=N\), so \(N\) is prime.

The following table supplies the needed modular computations. In a row with entries \(N,b\), the factorization shown is that of \(N-1\); the listed value \(R_q\) is
\[
R_q\equiv b^{(N-1)/q}\pmod N,
\qquad 0\le R_q<N.
\]
In every row, direct repeated-squaring also gives \(b^{N-1}\equiv1\pmod N\), and the last entries record that \(\gcd(R_q-1,N)=1\) for every listed \(q\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
N&b&N-1&q&R_q\pmod N\\ \hline
23&5&2\cdot11&2,11&22,2\\
37&2&2^2\cdot3^2&2,3&36,26\\
43&3&2\cdot3\cdot7&2,3,7&42,36,41\\
641&3&2^7\cdot5&2,5&640,357\\
277&5&2^2\cdot3\cdot23&2,3,23&276,116,27\\
42307&3&2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641&2,3,11,641&42306,36715,17937,10961\\
116341&14&2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277&2,3,5,7,277&116340,50801,81650,10889,35125
\end{array}
\]

For clarity, in each row the assertion about gcds means that subtracting \(1\) from every entry in the last column and applying the Euclidean algorithm with \(N\) gives gcd \(1\). These are finite integer calculations. The base primes \(2,3,5,7,11\) are immediate by trial division. The first row consequently proves that \(23\) is prime. The row for \(277\) may then use the already established primality of \(23\); the row for \(641\) uses only \(2\) and \(5\). The row for \(42307\) then uses the established primality of \(641\), and the row for \(116341\) uses that of \(277\). The rows for \(37\) and \(43\) prove their primality as well. Thus there is no circularity in these checks, and the five factors in (4) really are distinct primes. In particular they are pairwise coprime.

By (1), (2), and (3), the gcd-sum at the number in (4) is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n)=G(n)
 &=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
   (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
 &=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The arithmetic can be followed through the successive products
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Consequently
\[
A(n)=610815156979325.                                                        \tag{5}
\]
Adding \(1\) gives
\[
1+A(n)=610815156979326.
\]
But direct multiplication using the value of \(n\) gives
\[
26n=26\cdot23492890653051=610815156979326.                                  \tag{6}
\]
Thus \(n\mid 1+A(n)\). It follows that
\[
\gcd(n,1+A(n))=\gcd(n,26n)=n,
\]
and hence
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+A(n))}=\frac nn=1.                                 \tag{7}
\]

Finally, this \(n\) is neither \(1\) nor prime. It is plainly larger than \(1\), and (4), or simply
\[
23492890653051=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
expresses it as a product of two integers strictly between \(1\) and itself. Therefore it is composite.

We have found a positive composite integer \(n=23492890653051\) for which \(a(n)=1\). Hence the assertion that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime is false.
